newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says no reason for conflict with Syria.
newsitem.headline: Israel says no reason for conflict with Syria.

text.p: Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said on Friday there was no need for conflict between Syria and the Jewish state.

"I think that the Syrians understand that the way...is to come to the negotiating table and find ways to solve the conflicts peacefully and without confrontations," Mordechai told Israel's Channel One television. "That is our way. That is the way in which I am leading."

The announcement came a day after Syria said it would not agree to fresh peace talks with Israel until hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, elected in May, accepted all the understandings reached with the Jewish state's previous government.

Earlier on Friday Israeli helicopters rocketed suspected Hizbollah targets in southern Lebanon, heightening fear that it might mount a broad military offensive. Syria is the main power-broker in Lebanon, with an estimated 35,000 troops deployed across the country.

Asked about reports of recent Syrian troop movements in Lebanon, Mordechai said: "I do not think there are risks. There are all sorts of operations implemented in Syria. We follow them. We are doing what needs to be done."
Witnesses said on Thursday that Syria had redeployed troops in Beirut and other parts of the country.

Last month, Syrian troops also left a number of positions in the central Lebanese mountains, in what Lebanese security sources said was a defensive redeployment following apparent Israeli threats to attack Syrian forces in Lebanon.
Mordechai lauded his country's troops, who on Friday ambushed pro-Iranian Hizbollah guerrillas, killing one of them. The rocket attack followed the clash.
Israel occupies a 15 km (nine mile)-wide strip of south Lebanon as a self-declared security zone to protect its northern border.

Syrian-Israeli peace talks have been stalled over withdrawal from the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in 1967. Netanyahu has rejected concessions on the strategic plateau and called for unconditional talks.
